hints: Calculate the total number of equally likely outcomes when an 8-sided die is thrown twice: $8 \times 8 = 64$.
List the pairs where the scores differ by exactly $3$: $(x, x+3)$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$.
Remember that either the first die or the second die can have the larger score, doubling the number of favourable pairs.
walkthrough:
Determine the total number of equally likely outcomes in the sample space for two throws of a fair eight-sided die:
$$n(S) = 8 \times 8 = 64$$

Enumerate all ordered pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ where one score is exactly $3$ greater than the other ($|x_1 - x_2| = 3$):
$$\begin{aligned}
x_2 - x_1 = 3: & \quad (1,4), (2,5), (3,6), (4,7), (5,8) && (5 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 - x_2 = 3: & \quad (4,1), (5,2), (6,3), (7,4), (8,5) && (5 \text{ pairs})
\end{aligned}$$

Count the total number of favourable outcomes and calculate $\mathrm{P}(R)$:
$$n(R) = 5 \times 2 = 10$$
$$\mathrm{P}(R) = \frac{10}{64} = \frac{5}{32}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Throwing two 8-sided dice gives $8 \times 8 = 64$ equally likely pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ in the sample space:
$$\text{Total outcomes} = 8 \times 8 = 64$$

Event $R$ happens when the difference between the two scores is exactly 3 ($|x_1 - x_2| = 3$). List the pairs where the first score is 3 higher, or the second score is 3 higher:
$$\text{Pairs where } x_2 - x_1 = 3: (1,4), (2,5), (3,6), (4,7), (5,8) \to 5\text{ pairs}$$
$$\text{Pairs where } x_1 - x_2 = 3: (4,1), (5,2), (6,3), (7,4), (8,5) \to 5\text{ pairs}$$

Count the total successful pairs and divide by 64 to get the probability:
$$\mathrm{P}(R) = \frac{5 + 5}{64} = \frac{10}{64} = \frac{5}{32}$$

hints: The condition for event $S$ requires the product of the two scores to exceed $19$: $x_1 x_2 > 19$.
Notice that if the first die lands on $1$ or $2$, the maximum possible product is $2 \times 8 = 16 \le 19$, so no favourable pairs exist for $x_1 \in \{1, 2\}$.
Systematically list the valid second scores $x_2$ for each first score $x_1 \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$.
Sum the favourable outcomes and divide by the total number of outcomes, $64$.
walkthrough:
Analyze the condition for event $S$, which requires the product of the two scores to satisfy:
$$x_1 x_2 > 19$$
Since each score is an integer from $1$ to $8$, the maximum product when $x_1 \in \{1, 2\}$ is $2 \times 8 = 16 \le 19$. Hence, only throws with $x_1 \ge 3$ can satisfy the condition.

Systematically list all ordered pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ having product strictly greater than $19$ for each first die score:
$$\begin{aligned}
x_1 = 3: & \quad (3,7), (3,8) && (2 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 = 4: & \quad (4,5), (4,6), (4,7), (4,8) && (4 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 = 5: & \quad (5,4), (5,5), (5,6), (5,7), (5,8) && (5 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 = 6: & \quad (6,4), (6,5), (6,6), (6,7), (6,8) && (5 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 = 7: & \quad (7,3), (7,4), (7,5), (7,6), (7,7), (7,8) && (6 \text{ pairs}) \\
x_1 = 8: & \quad (8,3), (8,4), (8,5), (8,6), (8,7), (8,8) && (6 \text{ pairs})
\end{aligned}$$

Sum the favourable outcomes and compute the probability $\mathrm{P}(S)$:
$$n(S) = 2 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 6 = 28$$
$$\mathrm{P}(S) = \frac{28}{64} = \frac{7}{16}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Event $S$ happens when the product of the two scores is strictly greater than 19 ($x_1 \times x_2 > 19$). Let us systematically check possible values of $x_1$:
- If $x_1 = 1$ or $2$, maximum product is $2 \times 8 = 16$ (no pairs)
- If $x_1 = 3$: $x_2 \in \{7, 8\} \to 2\text{ pairs}$
- If $x_1 = 4$: $x_2 \in \{5, 6, 7, 8\} \to 4\text{ pairs}$
- If $x_1 = 5$: $x_2 \in \{4, 5, 6, 7, 8\} \to 5\text{ pairs}$
- If $x_1 = 6$: $x_2 \in \{4, 5, 6, 7, 8\} \to 5\text{ pairs}$
- If $x_1 = 7$: $x_2 \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\} \to 6\text{ pairs}$
- If $x_1 = 8$: $x_2 \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\} \to 6\text{ pairs}$

Sum the number of successful pairs across all possible values of $x_1$:
$$\text{Total pairs for } S = 2 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 6 = 28$$

Divide by 64 to find the probability of event $S$:
$$\mathrm{P}(S) = \frac{28}{64} = \frac{7}{16}$$

hints: Two events $R$ and $S$ are independent if and only if $\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$.
Find the intersection $R \cap S$ by testing which of the $10$ pairs in event $R$ have a product greater than $19$.
Calculate $\mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$ using your answers to parts (i) and (ii), and compare it directly with $\mathrm{P}(R \cap S)$.
walkthrough:
State the formal condition for two events to be independent:
$$R \text{ and } S \text{ are independent} \iff \mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$$

Find the intersection $R \cap S$ by examining which outcomes from the $10$ pairs in event $R$ also satisfy $x_1 x_2 > 19$:
$$\begin{aligned}
(1,4) \to 4, & \quad (4,1) \to 4 \\
(2,5) \to 10, & \quad (5,2) \to 10 \\
(3,6) \to 18, & \quad (6,3) \to 18 \\
(4,7) \to 28 > 19, & \quad (7,4) \to 28 > 19 \quad \checkmark \\
(5,8) \to 40 > 19, & \quad (8,5) \to 40 > 19 \quad \checkmark
\end{aligned}$$
Thus, $R \cap S = \{(4,7), (5,8), (7,4), (8,5)\}$, giving exactly $4$ outcomes:
$$\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \frac{4}{64} = \frac{1}{16}$$

Compute the product of the individual probabilities $\mathrm{P}(R)$ and $\mathrm{P}(S)$:
$$\mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S) = \frac{10}{64} \times \frac{28}{64} = \frac{5}{32} \times \frac{7}{16} = \frac{35}{512}$$

Compare the values and state the conclusion:
$$\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \frac{4}{64} = \frac{32}{512} \ne \frac{35}{512} = \mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$$
Since $\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) \ne \mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$, events $R$ and $S$ are not independent.
teacher_walkthrough:
Remember the test for independence: two events $R$ and $S$ are independent if and only if the probability of both happening together equals the product of their separate probabilities:
$$\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S)$$

Find the outcomes that belong to both $R$ and $S$ by checking which of the 10 pairs from event $R$ have a product greater than 19:
- $(4,7)$ and $(7,4)$ have product $28 > 19$ (2 pairs)
- $(5,8)$ and $(8,5)$ have product $40 > 19$ (2 pairs)
All other pairs in $R$ have products $\le 18$. So there are exactly 4 pairs in $R \cap S$:
$$\mathrm{P}(R \cap S) = \frac{4}{64} = \frac{1}{16} = \frac{32}{512}$$

Multiply the individual probabilities from parts (i) and (ii):
$$\mathrm{P}(R) \times \mathrm{P}(S) = \frac{10}{64} \times \frac{28}{64} = \frac{5}{32} \times \frac{7}{16} = \frac{35}{512}$$
Compare the two numbers: because $\frac{32}{512} \ne \frac{35}{512}$, the condition fails, so $R$ and $S$ are not independent.
